title.en: Practice: Reading a passage: the main idea and what is actually said
title.hi: अभ्यास: गद्यांश पढ़ना: मुख्य विचार और वास्तव में क्या कहा गया है

section: Practice (written by us, not from a UPSC paper): Reading a passage: the main idea and what is actually said

en.stem:
Cities are warmer than the countryside around them because concrete and asphalt absorb heat during the day and release it at night. Trees reduce this effect in two ways: their shade keeps surfaces cool, and water evaporating from their leaves cools the air. Yet a tree planted today gives little shade for several years. A city that wants cooler streets a decade from now must therefore plant now and, just as important, protect the mature trees it already has. Counting saplings planted says little; what matters is how many trees survive.

Passage 1. Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Trees cool the air because water evaporates from their leaves
Cities should stop using concrete and asphalt
To have cooler streets later, a city must plant now, protect its mature trees, and judge success by survival
Cities are always warmer than villages
en.why: The third option covers the whole passage, including its last sentence. The first is a supporting detail, the second is not said, and the fourth is only the opening fact with always added.

Passage 1. According to the passage, why does the number of saplings planted say little?
options: Because what matters is how many trees survive
Because saplings absorb heat during the day
Because cities plant too few saplings
Because mature trees do not give shade
en.why: The last sentence says this directly. The other options are not in the passage; the fourth contradicts it.

Cities are warmer than the countryside around them because concrete and asphalt absorb heat during the day and release it at night. Trees reduce this effect in two ways: their shade keeps surfaces cool, and water evaporating from their leaves cools the air. Yet a tree planted today gives little shade for several years. Counting saplings planted says little; what matters is how many trees survive.

Passage 1. Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
options: Saplings cool a street more than mature trees do
Planting trees has no effect on city heat
Asphalt releases heat only during the day
A city that replaces mature trees with the same number of saplings will have less shade for some years
en.why: A newly planted tree gives little shade for several years, so replacing mature trees with saplings reduces shade in that period. The others contradict the passage.

en.stem:
Reading a long book asks for something that scrolling through short messages does not: staying with one line of thought for an hour. This is a skill, and like other skills it weakens when it is not used. People who say they can no longer finish a book have usually not lost the ability; they have stopped practising it. The remedy is modest. Reading for twenty minutes at a fixed time each day, with the phone in another room, rebuilds the habit within weeks. The difficulty felt at the start is a sign of lost practice, not of a lack of ability.

Passage 2. Which of the following best expresses the crux of the passage?
options: Phones have destroyed the ability to read
Sustained reading is a skill that weakens without practice and returns with regular practice
Twenty minutes is the right length for reading
Short messages are easier to read than books
en.why: The passage says the ability is not lost, only unpractised, and gives a way to rebuild it. The first option is too strong, the third is a detail of the remedy, and the fourth is not the point.

Passage 2. According to the passage, the difficulty felt at the start of reading again shows:
options: That the book is badly written
That the reader lacks ability
That twenty minutes is too long
That the reader has lost practice
en.why: The last sentence: a sign of lost practice, not of a lack of ability. The second option is exactly what the author denies.

Passage 2. Which of the following is NOT supported by the passage?
options: A skill weakens when it is not used
Reading at a fixed time each day helps rebuild the habit
Short messages should be given up altogether
Many who cannot finish a book have stopped practising
en.why: The passage asks only that the phone be in another room during the twenty minutes. It nowhere says that short messages should be given up. The other three are stated.

en.stem:
A field that receives only chemical fertiliser year after year may keep giving good harvests for a time. The fertiliser supplies the main nutrients a crop needs. It does not supply organic matter, which holds water in the soil and feeds the organisms that keep soil loose. As organic matter falls, the soil hardens, holds less water and needs more fertiliser for the same yield. The farmer sees rising costs before seeing falling harvests. Returning crop residue and manure to the field is slower than adding fertiliser, but it treats the cause.

Passage 3. Which of the following is the main idea of the passage?
options: Using only chemical fertiliser slowly lowers the soil's organic matter and raises costs; returning organic matter treats the cause
Chemical fertiliser should never be used
Organic matter holds water in the soil
Farmers do not notice changes in their soil
en.why: The first option follows the passage from problem to remedy. The second is too strong: the passage objects to fertiliser alone. The third is a detail. The fourth is not said.

en.stem:
A field that receives only chemical fertiliser year after year may keep giving good harvests for a time. The fertiliser supplies the main nutrients a crop needs. It does not supply organic matter, which holds water in the soil and feeds the organisms that keep soil loose. As organic matter falls, the soil hardens, holds less water and needs more fertiliser for the same yield. The farmer sees rising costs before seeing falling harvests. Returning crop residue and manure to the field is slower than adding fertiliser, but it treats the cause.

Passage 3. According to the passage, what does organic matter do in the soil?
options: It supplies the main nutrients a crop needs
It holds water and feeds the organisms that keep the soil loose
It hardens the soil
It replaces the need for water
en.why: This is the third sentence in other words. The first option is what the passage says of fertiliser, not of organic matter.

en.stem:
A field that receives only chemical fertiliser year after year may keep giving good harvests for a time. The fertiliser supplies the main nutrients a crop needs. It does not supply organic matter, which holds water in the soil and feeds the organisms that keep soil loose. As organic matter falls, the soil hardens, holds less water and needs more fertiliser for the same yield. The farmer sees rising costs before seeing falling harvests. Returning crop residue and manure to the field is slower than adding fertiliser, but it treats the cause.

Passage 3. Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
options: Manure supplies more nutrients than chemical fertiliser
Hard soil gives higher yields
A farmer whose harvests are still good may already have a soil problem
Costs rise only after harvests fall
en.why: Harvests stay good for a time while organic matter falls, and costs rise before harvests fall. So good harvests do not show a healthy soil. The fourth option reverses the order given.

en.stem:
A public library is often judged by the number of books it lends. This misses much of what it does. For a student in a crowded home, the library is a quiet table. For a job-seeker, it is a computer and a connection. For an older person living alone, it is a place to be among others without having to buy anything. These uses leave no trace in lending records. A town that closes a library because lending has fallen may be measuring the wrong thing.

Passage 4. What is the central point of the passage?
options: Libraries should stop lending books
Older people use libraries more than students do
Fewer people read books today
Lending figures leave out much of what a library does, so decisions based on them alone may be mistaken
en.why: The passage opens with the usual measure, shows what it misses, and ends on the risk of measuring the wrong thing. The other options are not said.

en.stem:
A public library is often judged by the number of books it lends. This misses much of what it does. For a student in a crowded home, the library is a quiet table. For a job-seeker, it is a computer and a connection. For an older person living alone, it is a place to be among others without having to buy anything. These uses leave no trace in lending records. A town that closes a library because lending has fallen may be measuring the wrong thing.

Passage 4. Why does the author mention the student, the job-seeker and the older person?
options: To show who borrows the most books
To give examples of uses that lending records do not show
To argue that libraries need more computers
To prove that lending has fallen
en.why: The three are examples, and the next sentence says what they are examples of: uses that leave no trace in lending records.

en.stem:
A public library is often judged by the number of books it lends. This misses much of what it does. For a student in a crowded home, the library is a quiet table. For a job-seeker, it is a computer and a connection. For an older person living alone, it is a place to be among others without having to buy anything. These uses leave no trace in lending records. A town that closes a library because lending has fallen may be measuring the wrong thing.

Passage 4. Which of the following follows from the passage?
options: A fall in lending does not by itself show that a library is being used less
A library with low lending should always stay open
Lending records are false
Towns close libraries to save money
en.why: If several uses leave no trace in lending records, lower lending cannot alone show lower use. The second option is too strong, the third confuses incomplete with false, and the fourth gives a motive the passage does not mention.

en.stem:
Where water is supplied almost free, a user has little reason to repair a leaking tap or to choose a crop that needs less water. A price changes this. But a price that the poor cannot pay turns a need into a privilege. Some cities therefore charge in steps: a basic quantity at a very low rate, and higher rates for use beyond it. The design tries to serve two aims at once, access for all and care in use. Whether it succeeds depends on meters that work and bills that are collected.

Passage 5. Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Water should be free for everyone
Charging for water in steps tries to combine access with care in use, and works only if metering and billing work
The poor waste more water than the rich
Leaking taps are the main cause of water shortage
en.why: The passage sets two aims against each other, describes a design that serves both, and ends with the condition for success. The second option covers all three parts.

en.stem:
Where water is supplied almost free, a user has little reason to repair a leaking tap or to choose a crop that needs less water. A price changes this. But a price that the poor cannot pay turns a need into a privilege. Some cities therefore charge in steps: a basic quantity at a very low rate, and higher rates for use beyond it. The design tries to serve two aims at once, access for all and care in use. Whether it succeeds depends on meters that work and bills that are collected.

Passage 5. According to the passage, what is the drawback of supplying water almost free?
options: The poor cannot get water
Meters stop working
Users have little reason to save water
Bills are not collected
en.why: The first sentence says a user has little reason to repair a leak or choose a less thirsty crop. The first option is the drawback of a high price, not of a low one.

en.stem:
Where water is supplied almost free, a user has little reason to repair a leaking tap or to choose a crop that needs less water. A price changes this. But a price that the poor cannot pay turns a need into a privilege. Some cities therefore charge in steps: a basic quantity at a very low rate, and higher rates for use beyond it. The design tries to serve two aims at once, access for all and care in use. Whether it succeeds depends on meters that work and bills that are collected.

Passage 5. Consider these statements: 1. The price of water influences how carefully it is used. 2. Charging in steps always achieves both of its aims. Which of the statements is supported by the passage?
options: 1 only
2 only
Both 1 and 2
Neither 1 nor 2
en.why: Statement 1 is the point of the first two sentences. Statement 2 is too strong: the passage says the design tries to serve both aims and that success depends on meters and bills.
